title: Understanding Truncated Positional Encodings for Graph Neural Networks
one_liner: When graph neural networks use truncated positional encodings instead of complete ones, they lose expressive power in unexpected and different ways depending on the encoding type.
lead: Graph neural networks use positional encodings to help distinguish nodes in a graph—each node gets a list of numbers that encodes its position in the structure, letting the network tell similar nodes from different ones. Complete encodings use all the information available, but in practice, engineers truncate them to use only the first few strongest signals because computing all signals takes time proportional to the graph size cubed. This paper shows that truncation breaks the theoretical guarantees—different encoding types lose signal-spotting ability in different ways, and some become unable to recognize graph patterns they used to see.

paras: A graph neural network must learn which nodes are similar and which are different. Positional encodings are signals that attach to each node (a list of numbers per node) that encode where the node sits in the graph structure, so the network can distinguish nodes that play different roles. Two popular families—spectral (based on the graph's structural vibrations) and random walk (based on paths the network traces through the graph)—are mathematically proven to see the same range of patterns when used completely because both capture the full structural information just in different orders.

In practice, computing full encodings is expensive—work time and memory grow as you multiply the graph size by itself three times. So engineers always truncate them—use only the first k strongest signals instead of all n. Naive intuition says truncation just trades accuracy for speed, but the paper proves this is wrong: truncation changes what the network can see at all. Worse, spectral and random walk encodings degrade differently. A complete encoding might see the same patterns as its paired twin, but truncate both and they suddenly diverge.

callout.html: Truncated positional encodings lose different amounts of pattern-spotting ability depending on the encoding family, and spectral encodings drop to the level of a basic graph neural network.

steps.text: Compute all n signals for every node using spectral or random walk methods.
Check whether full encodings can distinguish node pairs using the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, a standard graph-comparison benchmark.
Keep only the top k strongest signals; drop the weaker k choices.
Test whether truncated encodings still distinguish the same node pairs and patterns.
Show that spectral and random walk methods degrade at different rates and reach different final expressivity levels.

paras: The paper changes which signals the network receives: from all n signals down to k signals chosen by strength. The object is the signal set itself—which positional encodings are kept vs. discarded.

hidden.name: expressivity ceiling after truncation
paras: Expressivity is the ceiling of patterns and distinctions a network can make. A network at the 1-WL level can perform simple graph comparisons; at the 3-WL level it can see more nuanced relationships. The Weisfeiler-Lehman test is a formal way to measure this ceiling. It asks: can the network distinguish every pair of structurally different node sets? The higher the WL level, the more patterns it sees.

The paper measures how far truncation pushes each encoding family down the expressivity ladder. Spectral encodings drop from somewhere between 1-WL and 3-WL all the way to 1-WL alone. Random walk encodings stay higher. This is the hidden quantity: where does each method land after truncation?

heat.caption: Darker means higher expressivity ceiling. Spectral always stops at 1-WL no matter k. Mixed methods reach the highest.

reads.html: After truncation, spectral encodings lose their edge and become indistinguishable from a basic graph network.
Truncated spectral positional encodings no longer exceed the 1-WL test expressivity, even with complete versions being 1-WL and 3-WL equivalent.

mechanism.h2: Why truncation breaks spectral but not random walk
paras: Spectral encodings are built from the graph's structural frequencies—like the natural vibrations of a drumhead. The first few frequencies (low-energy modes) describe coarse, global structure: is the graph connected? Are there big clusters? Later frequencies (high-energy modes) capture fine detail: which specific nodes are neighbors? When you truncate and keep only the top few, you keep the big-picture frequencies but throw away the fine details. This is like looking at a photograph through thick frosting—you see whether it is bright or dark overall, but not which person is smiling.

Random walk encodings work differently. They are built from powers of the adjacency matrix: first you ask which nodes are one step away, then two steps, then three. These encode local neighborhood structure directly. The first few powers already carry the most useful information for distinguishing nodes. When you truncate, you are just stopping the journey earlier, but you have already collected the most important signals. The later powers add refinement but are not critical.

Because spectral modes are ordered by frequency, not by usefulness for node discrimination, truncation removes information the network actually needs. Random walk encodings are naturally ordered by distance-from-node, so truncation removes only gradually less-useful signals. That is why they degrade differently.

stages.s: Full graph: edges and node labels
Truncate: keep top k, drop the rest (loses fine detail)
Network tries to distinguish nodes with only coarse signals
Expressivity capped: can only see coarse patterns now

math.words: The expressivity level of truncated encodings depends on how many independent patterns can be distinguished. For spectral methods with k eigenvectors, the expressivity does not increase beyond 1-WL no matter how large k is. For random walk methods, expressivity improves with k. A mixed strategy averaging both encodings recovers higher expressivity.
math.equation:
expressivity(truncated_spectral, k) = 1-WL (constant for all k)
expressivity(truncated_random_walk, k) = min(k, between_1-WL_and_3-WL)
expressivity(mixed, k) = max(spectral_k, random_walk_k)
symbols: basic graph distinguishing power (nodes compared only by direct neighbors)
higher graph distinguishing power (nodes compared via multi-hop neighborhoods)
number of signals kept after truncation
encoding family based on graph vibration modes
encoding family based on step-by-step node reachability
combining both spectral and random walk signals

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Consider a graph where node A and node B are structurally different only in their fine-grained neighborhood details (the types of nodes at distance 3+).
Spectral truncated to k=3: keeps only coarse frequency modes. Cannot distinguish A and B. Result: 1-WL expressivity.
Random walk truncated to k=3: keeps 1-step, 2-step, 3-step neighborhoods. CAN distinguish A and B because 3-step detail is captured. Result: between 1-WL and 3-WL.
Mixed truncated to k=3: uses both methods. Random walk part catches the difference. Result: higher expressivity than spectral alone.

math.note: The equation shows that spectral truncation creates a hard expressivity ceiling, while random walk scales up gracefully, and mixing both recovers lost power.

charts.title: Spectral truncation
charts.note: Spectral encodings hit a wall and cannot improve with more signals because the signals are ordered by frequency (coarse-to-fine), not by usefulness for node discrimination; adding more fine frequencies does not help if the network lost the architectural ability to use them under truncation.

charts.title: Random walk truncation
charts.note: Random walk encodings improve steadily as more signals are added because signals are ordered by distance-from-node (1-hop, 2-hop, 3-hop), so each additional signal brings new structural information the network can directly use for node discrimination.

charts.title: Mixed strategy
charts.note: Combining both families recovers most of the power of complete encodings.

items.html: If you truncate spectral encodings, they drop to basic graph network power no matter how many signals you keep. Spectral truncation is inherently limited because the signal ordering (by frequency) does not align with usefulness for node discrimination.
The paper proves different encoding families degrade at completely different rates. Truncating to k=5 might preserve random walk power but wreck spectral power. No universal answer.
Even closely related spectral variants like k-harmonic distances show different expressivity under truncation. Related does not mean identical.
Combining spectral and random walk signals (truncated) recovers most of the power of complete encodings at a fraction of the compute cost. This is the reliable strategy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph-classification task (e.g., predict whether a graph is a tree, cycle, or grid). Implement three node-encoding strategies: spectral truncated to k=5, random walk truncated to k=5, and mixed truncated to k=3 each. Train the same graph neural network backbone on each encoding. Run on a set of test graphs and measure the accuracy of node-pair discrimination (can the network tell apart nodes that should be different by structure?).
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss that random walk encodings retain discrimination power while spectral encodings hit a wall, and that mixing both recovers it.
